en: To accept or agree to something reluctantly but without protest
hook: ACQUIESCE: 'ACQUI-YES', saying a quiet yes.
story: Acquiesce. Nadia wanted to celebrate her twentieth birthday at a rooftop restaurant with her friends. Her parents insisted on a family dinner at home with every aunt and uncle. She argued. They insisted. Finally she sighed, said, "Fine," and helped her mother cook. She was not happy, but she did not fight. She acquiesced: accepted something reluctantly, without protest. Think of a quiet, unhappy yes. To acquiesce is to give in silently.

gre.s: Although she privately opposed the merger, the director chose to ____ rather than risk a damaging public battle with the board.
gre.clue: rather than risk a damaging public battle

example: Tired of arguing, the residents' committee acquiesced to the developer's plan to cut down two old mango trees.

en: To choose someone ceremonially for a role; to apply oil as part of a religious ceremony
bn: অভিষিক্ত করা; উত্তরাধিকারী হিসেবে মনোনীত করা
hook: ANOINT: kings were 'A-OIL-ed' — oil on the head at coronation.
story: Anoint. When the old headmaster of a famous Dhaka school announced his retirement, everyone wondered who would replace him. At the farewell assembly, he called young Mr. Imran to the stage, placed his own fountain pen in his hand, and declared him the next headmaster. He had anointed his successor: chosen him ceremonially for the role. Literally, to anoint is to rub with holy oil, as kings were anointed at coronations. Today the media anoint rising stars and front-runners.

gre.s: Although many party insiders expected an open contest, the retiring leader chose to ____ his deputy as successor, effectively ending the race before it began.
gre.clue: effectively ending the race before it began

example: Critics were quick to anoint the young Rajshahi novelist as the most important new voice of her generation.

en: A brief, clever saying that sums up a broad truth
hook: APHORISM: a short AFFIRMATION of truth.
story: Aphorism. Mitu's grandmother rarely gave long lectures. Instead, she offered short, wise sentences that stuck forever. "An empty pitcher makes the most noise." "The branch heavy with fruit bends low." Years later, Mitu still quotes them at the office. These were aphorisms: short, wise statements of a general truth. The word comes from the Greek for marking a boundary, the same root as horizon; an aphorism draws a sharp line around a truth. Synonyms: maxim, adage, proverb.

gre.s: The essay closes with a single pithy ____, "Certainty ages a face faster than doubt," which has been quoted far more often than any of the arguments that precede it.
gre.clue: a single pithy

example: Sticky notes bearing Tania's favourite aphorism, done is better than perfect, lined the edge of her computer monitor.

en: So confused that you cannot think clearly
hook: BE-FUDDLED: a brain in a MUDDLE.
story: Befuddled. On his first day in Tokyo, Arif stepped into Shinjuku Station. Thirteen train lines. Two hundred exits. Signs in Japanese. Three million people rushing past in every direction. He turned left, then right, then left again, then stood completely still, holding his map upside down. He was befuddled: utterly confused and perplexed. Think of a brain stuck in a muddle. Complicated tax forms leave many people befuddled.

gre.s: Students left the lecture thoroughly ____, as the professor had jumped between unrelated theories without explaining any of them.
gre.clue: without explaining any of them

example: Jet lag left the visiting scientist so befuddled that she gave her keynote talk with the slides in the wrong order.

en: To give a false impression of; to hide the truth behind an appearance
bn: ভুল ধারণা দেওয়া; আসল রূপ আড়াল করা
hook: BE-LIE: the appearance tells a LIE about what's underneath.
story: Belie. Tanvir walked out of the GRE center grinning and waving at his friends. "How was it?" they shouted. "Easy!" But in the rickshaw home, he put his head in his hands. He was sure he had failed the quant section. His cheerful face had told a lie about what he really felt. That is belie: an outward appearance that gives a false picture of the truth underneath. Remember it as be-lie: the surface tells a lie.

gre.s: The pianist's relaxed, almost careless stage manners ____ the punishing hours of practice that lie behind every performance.
gre.clue: relaxed, almost careless

example: The bakery's tiny, shabby storefront belies the remarkable quality of the pastries made inside.

en: Cheerfully carefree; casually indifferent to something serious
hook: BLITHE: BLISSfully unaware.
story: Blithe. Two days before his thesis was due, Shuvo was still singing in the hostel corridor, playing carrom, and planning a trip to Cox's Bazar. His roommate panicked on his behalf. Shuvo just smiled and said everything would work out. His attitude was blithe: cheerfully carefree, but dangerously indifferent to something serious. A blithe dismissal of a warning cheerfully ignores real danger. Blithe sounds light, like a bird singing, and that lightness is the point. Synonyms: carefree, nonchalant, heedless.

gre.s: The CEO's ____ dismissal of the auditors' warnings, delivered with a cheerful wave of the hand, alarmed investors who knew how serious the losses were.
gre.clue: delivered with a cheerful wave of the hand

example: Some commuters in Dhaka cross the busy road with blithe disregard for the buses roaring toward them.

en: Cautious; carefully considering all circumstances before acting
hook: CIRCUM-SPECT: looking (spect) all around (circum) before acting.
story: Circumspect. Before signing the lease for her first flat, Nadia read every clause twice, called the landlord's previous tenants, checked the water pressure in every tap, inspected the wiring, and asked a lawyer friend to review the contract. Her friends teased her for being paranoid. A year later, while their landlords cheated them, Nadia had no problems at all. She was circumspect: cautious, carefully considering every circumstance before acting. Circum means around, spect means look.

gre.s: Having been burned by a previous scandal, the senator was ____ in her public statements, weighing every word before she spoke.
gre.clue: weighing every word before she spoke

example: Journalists covering the election learned to be circumspect on the phone, assuming that every call might be monitored.

en: To cooperate secretly for a dishonest purpose
hook: COL-LUDE: playing (ludere) together secretly.
story: Collude. Three cement companies in one city met in secret and agreed to raise their prices together, so builders had no cheaper option. The government later fined them all. They had colluded: cooperated secretly for a dishonest purpose. The noun is collusion. Students who share answers during an online exam are colluding too. Col means together and ludere means to play, so to collude is to play together, but in a crooked game. Synonyms: conspire, connive, scheme.

gre.s: Investigators suspected that the two rival bidders had secretly agreed to ____, inflating their offers so that the government would pay far more than the project was worth.
gre.clue: secretly agreed

example: Officials found that several exam invigilators had colluded with a printing press to leak the question papers.

en: Feeling deep regret and guilt for having done wrong
hook: CONTRITE: sounds like 'contrition' — a confession full of regret.
story: Contrite. Rafi broke his mother's favourite glass bowl, the one from her wedding. Panicking, he hid the pieces in the garden. But that night he could not sleep. In the morning, eyes red, he confessed everything, apologized, and offered to buy a new one with his own savings. His mother hugged him. He was truly contrite: deeply sorry and full of guilt for his wrongdoing. Contrition is sincere, not just apologizing because you were caught.

gre.s: The defendant's ____ statement, in which he tearfully apologized to the victims, persuaded the judge to reduce his sentence.
gre.clue: tearfully apologized to the victims

example: The contrite striker visited the injured defender in hospital and apologized for his reckless tackle.

en: A formal or authoritative statement; a short saying
hook: DICTUM: what is DICTATED, spoken (dictus).
story: Dictum. Every new reporter at a Dhaka newspaper hears the same dictum from the chief editor on the first day: "If your mother says she loves you, check it out." He repeats it at every meeting until it becomes a reflex. A dictum is a formal or authoritative statement, often a short saying that guides practice. It comes from the Latin dicere, to say, as in dictate and dictionary. Courts also issue dicta, their formal remarks. Synonyms: maxim, pronouncement, edict.

gre.s: The founder's ____ that the customer is always right was treated by her managers as an unquestionable law, though she herself frequently ignored it.
gre.clue: treated by her managers as an unquestionable law

example: Architects still quote the famous dictum that form follows function, though few of their buildings actually obey it.

en: To extract the essential meaning; to purify a liquid by heating
hook: DISTILL: boil it down to the pure essence.
story: Distill. Mahin's thesis supervisor gave him a challenge: explain your two hundred pages of research in a single sentence. Mahin spent a whole evening cutting, rewriting, and cutting again, until only the core idea remained. He had distilled it: extracted its essential meaning. Literally, to distill is to purify a liquid by heating it into vapour and cooling it back down, the way distilled water is made. In both senses, you remove everything except the essence.

gre.s: In just a few pages, the author manages to ____ decades of complex research into a handful of clear principles that any reader can grasp.
gre.clue: into a handful of clear principles

example: Before kickoff, the coach distilled the whole match plan into three words on the whiteboard: press, pass, shoot.

en: To gradually intrude beyond proper limits
hook: EN-CROACH: like a COCKROACH creeping into your space.
story: Encroach. Each year, a factory beside a river near Dhaka moved its boundary wall a few meters closer to the water, filling the bank with sand and building new sheds. Environmental groups complained that it was encroaching on public land: gradually intruding beyond proper limits. Encroachment on rivers and footpaths is a constant problem in the city. The word comes from old French for catching with a hook, as if snatching land bit by bit. Synonyms: intrude, trespass, impinge.

gre.s: Residents worried that the expanding city would gradually ____ on the surrounding farmland, swallowing a few more fields each year until none remained.
gre.clue: swallowing a few more fields each year

example: Long working hours began to encroach on the evenings Babul had promised to spend with his children.

en: Lacking initiative or strength of character; irresponsible and ineffective
hook: FECK-LESS: 'feck' is old Scottish for effect. No effect at all.
story: Feckless. The new office manager never made decisions, never answered emails, and disappeared whenever a problem arose. When projects failed, he blamed his team. When clients complained, he forwarded the emails without comment. After six months, staff simply stopped asking him anything. He was feckless: irresponsible, lacking initiative, and ineffective. Feck is an old Scottish word for effect. Feckless means without any effect at all.

gre.s: Voters grew frustrated with the ____ government, which announced ambitious plans every year but never carried any of them out.
gre.clue: never carried any of them out

example: Her feckless brother borrowed money to start a new business every year and lost it within months.

en: Fussy and hard to please; requiring great attention to detail
hook: FINICKY: FINE details only — picky.
story: Finicky. Mitu's little brother is the most finicky eater in the family. He will not eat rice if it touches the dal. He removes every piece of onion from his curry and refuses fish if he spots a single bone. Feeding him takes an hour. Finicky means fussy and hard to please. It can also describe a task that needs great attention to detail, like repairing a finicky old watch. Synonyms: fussy, picky, fastidious. Its opposite is easygoing.

gre.s: The critic was notoriously ____ about food, sending back dishes whose sauce was a few degrees too cool or whose garnish sat slightly off centre.
gre.clue: sending back dishes whose sauce was a few degrees too cool

example: Orchids are finicky plants, so my aunt in Mymensingh checks the humidity in her greenhouse twice a day.

en: Secretive and sly, as if trying to avoid notice
hook: FURTIVE: like a FERRET, sneaking around quietly.
story: Furtive. In the middle of the exam, the invigilator noticed a boy in the third row. Every few minutes he glanced quickly at his left sleeve, then back at his paper, then nervously around the room. Glance, write, glance. She walked over and gently lifted his sleeve. Formulas were written on his wrist. His glances had been furtive: secretive and sly, trying to avoid notice, usually out of guilt. Picture a ferret sneaking quietly around.

gre.s: The thief cast ____ glances around the gallery before slipping the small sculpture into his coat.
gre.clue: before slipping the small sculpture into his coat

example: The two lovers exchanged furtive smiles across the crowded wedding hall, careful that no relative noticed.

en: Rude and cheeky in a bold, shameless way
hook: IM-PUDENT: no shame (pudor = shame).
story: Impudent. When Mahin's younger brother was told to finish his homework, he stuck out his tongue at their father, said, 'Do it yourself,' and walked away whistling. Their father was too shocked to speak. The boy's reply was impudent: shamelessly rude and disrespectful. Impudent comes from the Latin for without shame, the opposite of pudor, meaning modesty. Impudent and insolent are near twins. Synonyms: cheeky, impertinent, brazen.

gre.s: The ____ student not only ignored the teacher's warning but mimicked her voice in front of the whole class, apparently without the slightest shame.
gre.clue: apparently without the slightest shame

example: An impudent post from the club's official account mocked the referee and earned the team a heavy fine.

en: So clearly true that no one can argue against it
hook: IN-CONTROVERT-IBLE: NO CONTROVERSY possible.
story: Incontrovertible. For a year, the factory owner denied dumping chemicals into the river. Then a student journalist hid a camera on the bank. The footage showed the factory's pipe pouring black waste straight into the water, with a clear timestamp, and lab tests matched the chemicals. The evidence was incontrovertible: impossible to deny or dispute. Break it down: in means not, and controvert means to argue against, as in controversy. Synonyms: indisputable, irrefutable, undeniable. Opposite: questionable.

gre.s: Although the theory was once fiercely contested, the satellite data now provide ____ proof, leaving even the most skeptical scientists with no grounds for doubt.
gre.clue: leaving even the most skeptical scientists with no grounds for doubt

example: Carbon dating of the paper gave the museum incontrovertible proof that its prized manuscript was a modern forgery.

en: Having or showing great authority; sometimes domineering
hook: MAGISTERIAL: like a MAGISTRATE in court.
story: Magisterial. When Professor Ahmed entered the lecture hall, students stopped whispering immediately. He spoke slowly and with total certainty, never once looking at notes, and nobody dared interrupt. His thousand-page history of Bengal is considered the definitive work, quoted by every scholar. Both his manner and his book are magisterial: showing great authority. Sometimes magisterial suggests a domineering tone. Picture a magistrate in court, commanding the whole room.

gre.s: The historian's ____ survey of the empire, which drew on sources in twelve languages, is still regarded as the definitive work on the subject.
gre.clue: is still regarded as the definitive work

example: The retired judge gave a magisterial lecture on the constitution, speaking for two hours without a single note.

en: Done with minimal effort, routinely and without real interest
hook: PERFUNCTORY: done just to PERFORM the FUNCTION, nothing more.
story: Perfunctory. Imran's grandmother waited three hours to see the doctor. He glanced at her for one minute, asked two questions without looking up, scribbled a prescription, and called the next patient. He never read her test results. The checkup was perfunctory: done with minimal effort, routinely, without real interest. Think: done only to perform a function, nothing more. A perfunctory smile, a perfunctory apology, a perfunctory inspection.

gre.s: The manager gave the report only a ____ glance before signing it, a carelessness that allowed several glaring errors to slip through.
gre.clue: allowed several glaring errors to slip through

example: The waiter's perfunctory smile vanished the moment he turned away from our table.

en: To be the one who commits a crime or wrong
hook: PERPETRATE: a PERP (criminal) does it.
story: Perpetrate. For months, a gang in Sabbir's town sent fake lottery messages, telling people they had won a car and asking for a small processing fee. Hundreds of families lost money. When police finally arrested the men who had perpetrated the fraud, the town celebrated. To perpetrate is to carry out a harmful, illegal, or immoral act. The person who does it is the perpetrator. Do not confuse it with perpetuate, which means to keep something going. Synonyms: commit, carry out.

gre.s: Although the soldiers claimed they were only following orders, the tribunal held that those who ____ such atrocities bear personal responsibility for them.
gre.clue: the soldiers claimed they were only following orders

example: The bank's own IT manager perpetrated the fraud, quietly moving small sums into hidden accounts for six years.

en: Having a sad, longing sound, like a cry or lament
hook: PLAINTIVE: like a PLAINT, a sad complaint.
story: Plaintive. Late one night near the Padma, Tania heard a boatman singing a bhatiali song as he rowed home. His voice was slow and low, full of longing for a home and a love far away. Even without catching every word, she felt like crying. The song was plaintive: sounding sad and mournful. Plaintive shares a root with complaint and plaintiff: a plaintive sound is like a gentle lament. Synonyms: mournful, wistful, doleful. Its opposite is cheerful.

gre.s: From the abandoned house drifted the ____ notes of a flute, so sorrowful that passers-by stopped in the street and fell silent.
gre.clue: so sorrowful that passers-by stopped in the street and fell silent

example: Through the thin wall we heard the plaintive mewing of the neighbour's kitten, which had been shut out of the kitchen.

en: Strongly critical or controversial in argument
hook: POLEMICAL: POLE-vaulting into a fight; aggressive argument.
story: Polemical. A columnist wrote an article titled "Our Exam System Is Destroying Children." It did not weigh both sides. It attacked teachers, coaching centres, and ministers with fierce, sweeping arguments. Within hours, hundreds of furious replies poured in. Some called it brave; others called it reckless. The article was polemical: aggressively argumentative, designed to attack an idea and provoke debate. A polemic is a strong verbal attack. Polemicists love a fight.

gre.s: Although the book's ____ tone alienated some readers, its fierce attack on the policy succeeded in sparking a national debate.
gre.clue: its fierce attack on the policy

example: The scientist's polemical blog posts against homeopathy won her many fans and a few angry lawsuits.

en: Slow and clumsy because of great weight; dull and laborious
hook: PONDEROUS: as heavy as a POUND of lead.
story: Ponderous. The old elephant at the zoo moved slowly and heavily, each step seeming to shake the ground. The word for this is ponderous: slow and clumsy because of great weight. Arif's thesis earned the same word from his supervisor. It ran to four hundred pages of long sentences, repeated points and heavy jargon, dull and laborious to read. Ponderous comes from the Latin pondus, weight, as in ponder, to weigh something in the mind. Synonyms: lumbering, plodding, labored.

gre.s: The biography's ____ prose, weighed down by endless digressions and dense footnotes, made it a chore to read despite the fascinating life it described.
gre.clue: weighed down by endless digressions and dense footnotes

example: Freight trains made a ponderous climb up the hill outside Srimangal, crawling past the tea gardens at walking speed.

en: To push someone or something down to a lesser place
hook: RELEGATE: sent back to the LEAGUE below.
story: Relegate. Lamia was the star of her university football team, until a new coach arrived who disliked her. He moved her to the bench, then to the reserve squad, and finally gave her the job of collecting balls. He had relegated her: moved her to a lower or less important position. In European football, a team that finishes last is relegated to a lower division. Re means back and legare means to send. Synonyms: demote, downgrade, consign.

gre.s: Although she was once celebrated as a pioneer, younger scholars now tend to ____ her work to footnotes, considering her methods hopelessly outdated.
gre.clue: considering her methods hopelessly outdated

example: Once the new laptops arrived, the old desktop computers were relegated to a dusty storeroom behind the canteen.

en: To refuse to accept or be associated with; to reject
hook: REPUDIATE: REPEL and DENY.
story: Repudiate. A video from fifteen years ago surfaced online: a famous politician making cruel jokes about poor people. Within hours, millions had shared it. The next morning he held a press conference. "Those views were wrong. I reject them completely, and I am ashamed of them." He had repudiated his past words: refused to accept or be associated with them. Repudiate means to reject firmly. A government may also repudiate a debt, refusing to pay it.

gre.s: Hoping to save his career, the candidate was quick to ____ the extremist group that had endorsed him, insisting he shared none of its views.
gre.clue: insisting he shared none of its views

example: In later life, the philosopher repudiated many ideas from his first book, calling them the errors of youth.

en: A speech in a play where one character thinks aloud while alone
hook: SOLI-LOQUY: SOLO speech (loqui = speak).
story: Soliloquy. In the drama club's production of Hamlet, Imran stood alone on the dark stage under a single spotlight. No other actor was present. He spoke the prince's thoughts aloud: "To be, or not to be." The audience heard everything going on in Hamlet's troubled mind. That speech is a soliloquy: a speech in which a character, alone, speaks his thoughts aloud. Solus means alone and loqui means to speak in Latin: speaking alone. Compare monologue, which may be addressed to others.

gre.s: Unlike a dialogue, in which characters respond to one another, a ____ lets the audience overhear a character's private reflections while he stands alone on stage.
gre.clue: while he stands alone on stage

example: In Macbeth's dagger soliloquy, the audience watches a man wrestle aloud with his own conscience on the eve of murder.

en: Seeming true or reasonable on the surface but actually false
hook: SPECIOUS: looks SPECIAL on the surface, but it's wrong underneath.
story: Specious. "I studied for twelve hours yesterday," Tanvir announced, "so I can take the whole week off." It sounded logical. He had worked hard, after all. But memory does not work that way; it needs daily practice, not one marathon. His argument was specious: it seemed reasonable on the surface but was actually wrong. Specious arguments are dangerous precisely because they fool smart people. Think: they look special, but underneath they are flawed.

gre.s: The argument appeared persuasive at first, but on closer inspection its reasoning proved ____, resting on a statistic that had been misread.
gre.clue: resting on a statistic that had been misread

example: The salesman's specious claim that the filter removed every virus fell apart as soon as a chemist tested it.

en: Full of strong, turbulent emotions; stormy
hook: TEMPESTUOUS: like a TEMPEST (violent storm).
story: Tempestuous. The two famous painters fell in love in Paris. Their relationship was legendary: wild declarations of love one week, slammed doors and broken plates the next. They separated four times and married twice. Friends never knew whether to buy them a wedding gift or a sympathy card. Their love was tempestuous: stormy, full of strong, turbulent emotions. A tempest is a violent storm at sea. Tempestuous weather, a tempestuous temper.

gre.s: The composer's ____ relationship with his patron, marked by violent quarrels and tearful reconciliations, inspired several of his most passionate works.
gre.clue: marked by violent quarrels and tearful reconciliations

example: The tempestuous final session of parliament ended with members shouting and tearing up copies of the budget.

en: Polished, sophisticated, and courteous
hook: URBANE: URBAN, city-polished manners.
story: Urbane. At the diplomatic dinner, the ambassador moved gracefully from guest to guest, switching effortlessly between English, French, Arabic, and Bangla. He remembered every name, told witty stories, and when a guest insulted his country, he smiled and replied with polite charm. Nobody could ruffle him. He was urbane: polished, sophisticated, and courteous, like a refined city dweller. Urbane shares a root with urban. Its opposite is boorish or uncouth.

gre.s: The ____ host, polished and witty, put even his most awkward guests at ease.
gre.clue: polished and witty

example: The urbane museum director chatted in French with the visiting minister and then in Bangla with the guards.

en: Remaining as a small trace of something that once was larger or more important
hook: VESTIGIAL: a VESTIGE, a remnant.
story: Vestigial. In biology class, Mahin learned that humans still have a tailbone, the tiny remains of a tail our distant ancestors once had. It no longer works as a tail at all. Such an organ is vestigial: remaining only as a small trace of something that was once larger or more important. A vestige is a trace, literally a footprint. In some countries the monarchy is vestigial, a ceremonial trace of old power. Synonyms: rudimentary, residual, leftover.

gre.s: Although the office of governor-general still exists, its powers are now largely ____: the post survives as a ceremonial remnant of an era when it truly governed.
gre.clue: survives as a ceremonial remnant

example: The town's vestigial city wall, now a few crumbling stretches, still marks where the medieval market once stood.
